title: In utero molecular correction of fetal-onset genetic disease

concept.text: The proposed innovation is durable treatment of disease-relevant fetal cells during an ongoing pregnancy, early enough to change the course of a genetic disease before irreversible injury occurs. The intended result is persistent molecular correction or functional replacement of the cells responsible for disease, with clinically meaningful benefit after birth and acceptable safety for both mother and fetus. This describes a target capability, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

Conceptual scope: the central requirement is lasting correction in the relevant cells. Delivering a treatment before birth is not sufficient by itself. A temporary supply of a missing protein may provide prenatal benefit without correcting the cells that cause the disease. Likewise, introducing donor stem cells demonstrates delivery and transplantation, but definitive treatment requires those cells to persist and contribute enough function to alter disease. The supplied alpha-thalassemia major trial illustrates this distinction: prenatal maternal-cell transplantation was feasible, but the reported low-level maternal microchimerism did not establish definitive correction.

Scope distinction: this is fetal therapy within an existing pregnancy. Editing an embryo in a laboratory, reading fetal genetic information for diagnosis, and supporting development with an artificial placenta address different capabilities. None substitutes for demonstrating durable correction of disease-relevant cells in a treated fetus.

significance.text: Conditional significance: for a disease in which irreversible injury develops before delivery, effective correction during fetal development could prevent damage that treatment after birth cannot undo. That would create a therapeutic opportunity unavailable after the injury has occurred. The magnitude of benefit depends on the disease, the timing of injury, and whether enough relevant cells can be corrected before that window closes. The supplied evidence does not establish this opportunity across every organ system originally listed in the research.

Alpha-thalassemia major provides a concrete example of prenatal therapeutic urgency. The supplied trial abstract describes a disease requiring serial in utero transfusions for survival and identifies a continuing need for definitive therapy. This supports the importance of treating at least some genetic diseases before birth, while leaving open whether a particular molecular intervention can prevent irreversible injury or replace ongoing supportive treatment.

Conditional downstream possibilities include reducing disease burden from birth, preventing complications that otherwise accumulate before postnatal treatment, and reducing dependence on repeated supportive interventions. These outcomes would require disease-specific demonstrations. Durable disease modification would be an important advance even if children retained symptoms or needed additional care; a disease-free child is a stronger outcome than the proposed completion threshold.

Impact boundary: prenatal intervention needs a meaningful advantage over treatment after delivery to justify its additional maternal and fetal demands. Diseases treated equally well after birth provide a weaker rationale. Success in one disease would not establish applicability across the brain, heart, skeleton, liver, and blood, because those tissues may require different delivery routes, treatment windows, and levels of correction. Neither broad clinical adoption nor inherited alteration of future generations follows automatically from successful fetal treatment.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unsolved target capability is reliable, persistent correction of enough disease-relevant fetal cells before injury becomes irreversible, with acceptable maternal and fetal safety. Proposed engineering requirements include reaching the correct tissue during an effective developmental window, achieving sufficient functional correction, and maintaining that benefit as the child grows. Delivery, timing, correction level, and persistence must work together; success on only one of these dimensions would not establish the full capability.

The supplied transplantation trial identifies a specific biological obstacle in alpha-thalassemia major. It reported low-level maternal microchimerism, meaning that maternal donor cells were present only at low levels, and linked expanded host progenitor populations to a possible competitive disadvantage for donor cells. Getting cells into the fetus therefore did not ensure that they could establish a sufficiently large functional population. The authors identified limitations of the tested protocol without concurrent bone marrow conditioning. This finding does not establish that conditioning would solve the problem or be acceptable during pregnancy.

Proposed safety requirements include avoiding injury from treatment and delivery, controlling the persistence and behavior of transplanted or modified cells, and detecting delayed adverse effects. The original concern about an uncontrolled graft is appropriately retained as a design concern rather than a harm demonstrated in the supplied trial. A small study described as safe and feasible cannot establish safety across different diseases, tissues, interventions, or longer follow-up periods.

The available evidence establishes a gap between feasible transplantation and definitive therapy in the inspected alpha-thalassemia major protocol. It does not establish that all in utero transplantation approaches have failed, or that durable fetal genetic correction remained undemonstrated throughout the field on November 1, 2026.

current_state.text: The July 28, 2026 Blood Advances report, cited as volume 10, pages 5003–5013, DOI 10.1182/bloodadvances.2026019655, describes transplantation of maternal CD34+ blood stem cells into six fetuses with alpha-thalassemia major at 23.1 ± 1.1 weeks of gestation. All also received serial prenatal transfusions. The abstract characterizes the protocol as safe and feasible while reporting low-level maternal microchimerism and limitations without concurrent bone marrow conditioning. These findings demonstrate feasibility of the tested prenatal transplantation procedure, not definitive genetic correction. The accompanying transfusions also matter when interpreting clinical outcomes.

The supplied review assessed the PubMed record and abstract rather than the full Blood Advances article. Its findings support the reported recipient count, gestational age, accompanying transfusions, limited donor-cell presence, and authors' conclusion. They do not provide a full assessment of detailed outcomes or long-term safety. Figure captions in the retained record do not substitute for examination of the figures or full report.

The accessible portion of the May 20, 2026 STAT article reported that MacKenzie's team had submitted an investigational new drug application for a proposed human fetal gene-therapy trial. This is more specific than the earlier account that an application was merely under discussion. The article described human fetal gene therapy as not yet realized at that date. Submission of an application does not establish authorization, treatment of a participant, or therapeutic success. The article was only partly accessible because of a paywall, and its May account cannot establish the field's status in November.

The original research described PEARL, linked to NCT04532047, as prenatal enzyme replacement for selected lysosomal diseases and assigned the registry an October 28, 2026 update date. The retained ClinicalTrials.gov content contained only generic interface text, so the supplied review could not verify the study identity, intervention details, or update date. These remain unverified assertions within this evidence package. Conceptually, temporary replacement of an enzyme would need to be distinguished from durable correction of disease-relevant cells even if it produced clinical benefit.

The original research also attributed to NIH RePORTER project 5R01HD110270-04 a report that a fetus with infantile Pompe disease received prenatal enzyme infusions and was born at term with normal cardiac function. The retained RePORTER extraction contained only a generic label, preventing verification of the project identity or outcome. The supplied review therefore does not establish that result, but the extraction failure is not evidence that the reported outcome is false. Even if verified, that outcome alone would not demonstrate durable fetal genetic correction.

Evidence boundary: the supplied materials do not establish published, durable correction of disease-relevant fetal cells, but they also do not establish its field-wide absence as of November 1, 2026. No bounded freshness search record was supplied. The dated transplantation findings and partially accessible news report should therefore be read as specific observations rather than a comprehensive account of every fetal gene-therapy program.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: a peer-reviewed clinical series in at least one fetal-onset genetic disease should show that treatment during pregnancy produces persistent correction of the relevant cells and a durable, clinically meaningful improvement through birth and early childhood. The evidence should connect the molecular or cellular change to disease modification, rather than relying only on successful delivery of a treatment or detection of a small number of donor cells. This is a proposed threshold, not an established consensus standard.
completion_criteria.label: Persistent correction yields clinically meaningful benefit through early childhood

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidence for reproducibility and attribution should include consistent results across treated patients, repeatable measurement of correction in the relevant cells or tissues, and interpretable clinical outcomes against the expected disease course or an appropriate comparison. Concurrent care, including prenatal transfusions or postnatal therapy, should be documented so its contribution can be distinguished from that of the prenatal correction. The supplied alpha-thalassemia major study, in which all recipients also received serial transfusions, illustrates why this distinction matters.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible correction and clinical outcomes distinguish prenatal treatment’s contribution

completion_criteria.text: Proposed breadth criterion: after an initial convincing demonstration, replication in a second disease with a different target tissue would test whether the capability extends beyond one biological setting. Additional independent replication would strengthen confidence. Such finite demonstrations would establish the tested breadth, not universal applicability to fetal genetic disease or every organ.
completion_criteria.label: Replication in a second disease targets a different tissue

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical and safety boundaries include a defined treatment window, reproducible delivery, sufficient persistent correction, and acceptable maternal and fetal outcomes. Follow-up should continue beyond early childhood to assess durability and delayed harms. Early-childhood benefit cannot establish lifelong correction or exclude late adverse effects. Disease modification may meet the proposed initial threshold without eliminating every symptom or subsequent treatment need.
completion_criteria.label: Defined treatment boundaries and safety follow-up beyond early childhood

completion_criteria.text: Temporary enzyme replacement alone, transient low-level graft chimerism without durable disease benefit, and laboratory embryo editing would not meet these criteria. Each may answer a useful scientific or therapeutic question, but none by itself demonstrates persistent molecular correction of disease-relevant cells in a fetus treated during an ongoing pregnancy.
completion_criteria.label: Transient effects and embryo editing cannot establish prenatal disease correction

related_concepts.text: Roster synthesis: OBG-03, Extrauterine physiological support across the viability gap, concerns sustaining development outside the uterus. It could conceivably change access for treatment delivery, but fetal molecular correction does not require that platform and would still need its own efficacy and safety evidence. OBG-08, A manufactured uterus that supports pregnancy without a donor graft and chronic immunosuppression, similarly addresses gestational support rather than correction of a fetal genetic disease.

Roster synthesis: OBG-04, In utero reversal of placental insufficiency, shares the objective of intervening during pregnancy before injury progresses, but targets placental dysfunction. OBG-10, Restoration of the amniotic compartment after preterm membrane rupture, targets the fetal environment and membrane-related loss of support. OBG-01, Causal control of the human parturition clock, targets the timing of labor. These capabilities could affect the circumstances or available duration of fetal treatment, but success in any one would not demonstrate durable correction of fetal disease cells.

Roster synthesis: OBG-02, Manufacture of a functional human oocyte from a somatic cell, and OBG-05, Reversal of human ovarian reproductive aging, concern reproductive capacity before pregnancy. Their connections to genetics and developmental biology do not make them demonstrations of treatment in an existing fetus. Embryo germline editing and prenatal genomic diagnosis are additional adjacent capabilities: one alters an embryo and the other supplies information, whereas OBG-06 requires a therapeutic effect during pregnancy.

Roster synthesis: OBG-07, A mechanism-based cure for endometriosis, and OBG-09, Fertility-preserving interception of high-grade serous tubo-ovarian carcinoma, concern maternal reproductive disease and preservation of reproductive function. They share a broad interest in intervening before lasting harm, but have different disease mechanisms, target tissues, treatment settings, and completion criteria. They remain distinct entries from fetal molecular correction.

change_log.reason: Maintains the concept identity and separates the target capability from adjacent prenatal procedures.

change_log.change: Replaced the field-wide claim that prenatal stem-cell transplantation has not produced a reliable cure with the disease- and protocol-specific findings of the alpha-thalassemia major trial.
change_log.reason: The inspected abstract supports limited engraftment and lack of definitive correction in that protocol, not a conclusion about every transplantation approach.

change_log.change: Restored the exact reported gestational age, maternal CD34+ cell source, six recipients, accompanying serial transfusions, low-level microchimerism, and possible donor-cell competitive disadvantage.
change_log.reason: These supported details explain both the demonstrated feasibility and the remaining biological barrier.

change_log.change: Corrected the STAT account from an application under discussion to a submitted investigational new drug application.
change_log.reason: The supplied review identifies submission in the accessible article text; submission does not establish trial authorization or treatment.

change_log.change: Retained the PEARL and Pompe assertions as explicitly unverified accounts and explained the registry and RePORTER extraction limitations.
change_log.reason: The retained content could not verify those specifics. Missing evidence does not establish that the assertions are false.

change_log.change: Reframed revolutionary significance as conditional prevention of prenatal injury and distinguished disease modification from complete cure.
change_log.reason: The proposed completion threshold does not require a disease-free child, and the supplied evidence does not establish irreversible injury across all originally named organs.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration to include fetal safety, attribution of benefit, reproducibility, continued follow-up, and practical treatment boundaries.
change_log.reason: Persistent molecular change, clinical benefit, and acceptable safety must be demonstrated together; early follow-up cannot establish lifelong durability.

change_log.change: Kept the two-disease demonstration as a proposed breadth criterion and explicitly limited its interpretation.
change_log.reason: The threshold is not a published standard, and finite successful tests cannot establish universal applicability.

change_log.change: Separated dated findings from a present-day field-wide conclusion and integrated distinctions across the supplied concept roster.
change_log.reason: The supplied freshness record is empty, while neighboring reproductive and gestational capabilities have different targets and evidence requirements.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish whether durable human fetal genetic correction had been demonstrated anywhere by November 1, 2026; no bounded freshness search record was supplied.
The PEARL study identity, intervention details, and claimed October 28, 2026 registry update remain unverified because the retained registry extraction lacked study-specific content.
The NIH project identity and reported Pompe outcome remain unverified because the retained RePORTER extraction lacked project-specific content.
The full Blood Advances article was not assessed in the supplied review, limiting evaluation of detailed outcomes, safety, and follow-up beyond the abstract.
The partly accessible STAT report does not establish the subsequent regulatory disposition of the submitted application or whether treatment later occurred.
Disease-specific treatment windows, required correction levels, feasible delivery routes, and acceptable safety boundaries remain to be established.

The original list of prenatal injury across brain, heart, skeleton, liver, and blood lacks supporting disease-specific evidence in this package; it was retained only as a limit on extrapolation, not as an established anatomical claim.

brief.title: Lasting treatment of genetic disease before birth
possible: A child with a genetic disease that causes damage before birth could receive lasting treatment during pregnancy. Correcting the cells responsible, or replacing their function, could prevent irreversible injury and keep helping after birth.
why: For families facing these diseases, treatment during pregnancy could reach a window that closes before delivery. Children could begin life with less damage and less need for repeated supportive treatment.

sources.showed: Six fetuses received blood-forming cells from their mothers alongside prenatal blood transfusions. Maternal microchimerism, the presence of maternal donor cells, remained low.
sources.quote: Low-level maternal microchimerism was detected in all recipients;
sources.cited_for: Transplanting maternal cells before birth was feasible, but donor cells remained scarce.
sources.not_established: The treatment did not establish lasting correction sufficient to change the disease.

sources.showed: This is a study protocol for replacing missing proteins before birth in selected inherited diseases.
sources.cited_for: It represents prenatal protein replacement as a treatment approach.
sources.not_established: Temporary protein replacement alone does not establish lasting correction of disease-causing cells.

sources.who: Researchers studying prenatal treatment of Pompe disease
sources.showed: This is a project description concerning prenatal infusions of a missing protein for infantile Pompe disease.
sources.cited_for: It concerns treating an inherited disease during pregnancy through protein replacement.
sources.not_established: A favorable outcome at birth alone would not establish lasting correction of the relevant cells.

sources.who: Tippi MacKenzie and her research team
sources.showed: The team treated inherited diseases in mice before birth using gene replacement, which supplies working genes. It also submitted an application for a human fetal trial.
sources.quote: They cured mice with hemophilia and mice with tyrosinemia.
sources.cited_for: Animal results and an application for a human trial support the path toward fetal gene treatment.
sources.not_established: An application does not establish permission to proceed, treatment of a participant, or human benefit.

shown: MacKenzie's team transplanted maternal blood-forming cells into fetuses with alpha-thalassemia major, an inherited blood disease requiring transfusions before birth for survival. Outcomes around birth were broadly similar to transfusions alone. The small study supported feasibility, but did not establish definitive treatment.
missing: Enough relevant cells must receive lasting correction before irreversible injury begins.
Corrected or replacement cells must keep functioning as the child grows.
Treatment must provide meaningful benefit with acceptable safety for both mother and fetus.

milestones.label: Lasting correction improves health through early childhood
milestones.explanation: A peer-reviewed clinical series would have to link persistent correction of relevant cells to meaningful benefit through early childhood. This would connect the cellular change to better health.

milestones.label: Repeated results reveal prenatal treatment's contribution
milestones.explanation: Results would have to repeat across patients, with reliable cell measurements and comparisons that distinguish prenatal correction from other care. This would establish how much benefit the correction provides.

milestones.label: Success extends to another disease and tissue
milestones.explanation: A second disease affecting a different tissue would have to show convincing results. This would test whether the capability extends beyond its first biological setting.

milestones.label: Treatment boundaries and longer-term safety become clear
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to define treatment timing, reliable delivery, sufficient lasting correction and acceptable safety, with follow-up beyond early childhood. This would test durability and reveal delayed harms.

milestones.label: Lasting fetal correction defines what counts
milestones.explanation: Temporary protein replacement, fleeting donor-cell presence or laboratory embryo editing alone would not qualify. Success requires lasting correction with disease benefit in a fetus treated during pregnancy.

uncertain: The treatment window, delivery route and amount of correction needed will depend on the disease and tissue.
Early-childhood benefit cannot establish lifelong correction or rule out late harms.
The proposed early-childhood threshold is not an agreed scientific standard.

page.title: In utero somatic gene and cell therapy
page.definition: Treatment given to a fetus during pregnancy provides a lasting source of a function impaired by a disease that begins before birth. Gene therapy restores that function in the child’s body cells. In cell therapy, donor cells engraft: they become established in the child and supply functional cells. Prenatal transplantation has restored donor-derived T cells in children with severe combined immunodeficiency. Repeated infusions of a missing enzyme supply the protein only.

goal.need: Fetuses with alpha-thalassemia major usually need transfusions to survive to birth. All six children in one prenatal transplant study still needed blood every two to four weeks after birth. Sufficient donor red-cell production could free a child from those transfusions. In a retrospective cohort of 60 children with early-onset GM1 gangliosidosis, median survival was 19 months. Treatment before birth could prevent nerve damage that is already irreversible by infancy. Both uses depend on timely diagnosis and an acceptable balance of benefit and risk for mother and fetus.

completion.title: FDA grants traditional approval to a gene or cell therapy with an explicit prenatal indication.
completion.criterion: FDA grants traditional biologics licence approval for at least one gene or engrafting-cell product administered in utero for a fetal-onset genetic disease. The product establishes persistent gene function or donor-cell function. Its evidence meets safety, purity and potency requirements and demonstrates clinical benefit, or an effect on a validated surrogate endpoint, for the labelled prenatal use. Efficacy thresholds and follow-up are those accepted for that product and disease.
completion.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration: biological-product licensing requirements and the August 2026 cellular and gene therapy guidance, applied to an explicit prenatal indication.
completion.threshold_quote: FDA approval to market a biologic is granted by issuance of a biologics license.
completion.basis: FDA licensure supplies an external decision about clinical use and manufacturing. Traditional approval requires clinical benefit or a validated surrogate. This completion test uses that established pathway for a prenatal indication. FDA’s cited guidance supplies no universal corrected-cell percentage or minimum duration of benefit.

milestones.title: A fetal therapy shows biological activity and feasible administration in preclinical studies.
milestones.criterion: Preclinical studies demonstrate biological activity of the investigational product and the feasibility of its intended prenatal route of administration. For gene therapy, the IFeTIS consensus calls for reproducible evidence from prenatal studies in an appropriate animal model of the disease.
milestones.set_by: FDA, August 2026 cellular and gene therapy guidance, question 27; IFeTIS’s 2019 consensus adds disease-model requirements specifically for gene therapy.
milestones.threshold_quote: evaluate bioactivity, determine the feasibility of the ROA

milestones.title: A fetal gene or cell therapy is administered in an early-phase human study.
milestones.criterion: At least one fetus receives the investigational gene or cell product during an ongoing pregnancy in an early-phase clinical study. Safety is a primary outcome, with monitoring of both the pregnant participant and the fetus.
milestones.set_by: FDA early-phase cellular and gene therapy guidance, section I, and the IFeTIS consensus on maternal and fetal safety in initial trials.
milestones.threshold_quote: initial introduction of an investigational new drug into humans

milestones.title: An early human study characterizes the active dose range or the safety of the feasible dose.
milestones.criterion: An early-phase trial characterizes the range of biologically active or optimal effective doses against its prespecified activity and toxicity measures. When production or delivery limits the doses that can be given, the trial establishes the specified target exposure or characterizes safety at the feasible dose or doses.
milestones.set_by: FDA guidance on early-phase cellular and gene therapy trials, section IV.A.1, Dose Exploration.
milestones.threshold_quote: characterizing the safety profile of the feasible dose or doses

milestones.title: Human studies establish substantial evidence that a fetal therapy benefits its target disease.
milestones.criterion: Two adequate and well-controlled clinical investigations, or one such investigation plus confirmatory evidence when FDA accepts that combination, establish effectiveness for the proposed prenatal indication. The endpoint measures how the patient feels, functions or survives, or is a validated surrogate for that benefit. The effect size, analysis and follow-up are specific to the disease and product.
milestones.set_by: FDA, August 2026 cellular and gene therapy guidance, questions 32–34; these are general biological-product effectiveness criteria.
milestones.threshold_quote: one adequate and well-controlled clinical study plus confirmatory evidence is sufficient to establish effectiveness.

milestones.title: Studies provide enough evidence to assess risk to both the pregnant patient and the fetus.
milestones.criterion: Before enrollment, the available studies provide a basis for assessing maternal and fetal risks from both the product and its administration. For research covered by 45 CFR 46.204(a), the evidence includes, where scientifically appropriate, preclinical studies in pregnant animals and clinical studies in nonpregnant women.
milestones.set_by: US Department of Health and Human Services, 45 CFR 46.204(a), for research covered by Subpart B. The IFeTIS safety consensus addresses risks from both the product and its administration.
milestones.threshold_quote: provide data for assessing potential risks to pregnant women and fetuses

milestones.title: The prenatal product meets its prespecified measure of biological activity in a human recipient.
milestones.criterion: The recipient meets the study’s product-specific activity endpoint at the specified assessment. For alpha-thalassemia major in NCT02986698, the engraftment endpoint is at least 1% maternal donor cells in the recipient’s circulation. The protocol specifies cord blood at birth, or assessment at 40 weeks’ corrected gestational age after preterm delivery, then weekly measurements for four weeks and monthly measurements for one year to assess stability.
milestones.set_by: FDA early-phase guidance, section IV.A.3, identifies activity measures. UCSF protocol NCT02986698 sets the numerical endpoint and schedule for alpha-thalassemia major.
milestones.threshold_quote: donor cell chimerism equal to or greater than 1% donor cells in the circulation of the fetal recipient.

not_found: No cross-disease minimum corrected-cell fraction or duration of clinical benefit was found in the IFeTIS consensus, FDA guidance or fetal protocols searched.
No FDA licence explicitly authorising prenatal gene or engrafting-cell treatment was identified in the FDA product and programme sources searched.
The current FDA disposition of the GM1 prenatal gene-therapy IND was not established by the accessible public documents.
Direct ClinicalTrials.gov study pages and API requests, and NIH RePORTER project 11095794, did not yield readable study or project text.

results.finding: Among six maternal–fetal pairs receiving prenatal transplantation, two mothers received prophylactic antibiotics after positive cell cultures.
results.detail: The report includes maternal hemoglobin monitoring around marrow harvest and fetal and perinatal follow-up at the administered dose.
results.quote: Two mothers received prophylactic antibiotics because of late positive cultures of harvested cells (without fetal adverse events).

results.finding: Low-level maternal microchimerism was detected in all six prenatal transplant recipients.
results.detail: The reported T-cell response measures reactivity to maternal antigens and does not quantify the circulating maternal donor-cell fraction.

results.finding: The six prenatal transplant recipients had no significant perinatal differences versus the transfusion-only cohort.
results.detail: Both cohorts received prenatal transfusions. The supplied text gives no sample size for the transfusion-only cohort.
results.quote: Perinatal outcomes were broadly similar to those undergoing IUT alone.

results.finding: Prenatal gene replacement reportedly cured mice across 2 disease models. The number of mice was unreported.
results.detail: These were earlier experiments in hemophilia and tyrosinemia. The proposed human trial targets a lysosomal storage disorder.
results.quote: Over and over it worked. They cured mice with hemophilia and mice with tyrosinemia.

results.finding: FDA reportedly allowed UCSF to bypass animal testing for a study planned for 5 fetuses, citing prior vector safety work. Prior study sizes were unreported.
results.detail: STAT reports the FDA communication. The supplied text contains no official decision or underlying safety data.
results.quote: The agency told them they could bypass animal testing, because the safety profile of the vector they plan to use already has been so well characterized by other academics and companies developing gene therapies for kids and adults.

results.finding: All five fetal AAV9-GBA-treated mice with neuronopathic Gaucher disease survived to day 70.
results.detail: Some brain and visceral pathology persisted after treatment. The macaques received a reporter vector to test delivery.
results.quote: In contrast, at 70 days of age all treated knockouts appeared normal and fertile, two were able to produce a litter of two symptomatic knockouts (

results.finding: Both of the two fetal macaques given prenatal intracerebroventricular AAV9 reporter vector appeared normal at birth.
results.detail: Follow-up ended on postnatal days 0 and 6. The paper reports no clinical safety data in nonpregnant women for this product.
results.quote: Both macaques presented normally at birth.

results.finding: Fancd2-null Fanconi anemia mice (n=3) averaged 26.9% donor granulocyte chimerism four weeks after prenatal transplantation.
results.detail: Bone marrow collected at 48 weeks showed resistance to mitomycin C and long-term reconstitution in secondary recipients.
results.quote:
The average donor granulocyte chimerism was 26.9% in
Fancd2
–/–
mice (n = 3), with only 3.5% and 2.0% in heterozygous
Fancd2
+/−
(n = 10) and WT (n = 5) littermates, respectively.

results.finding: In mice given prenatal donor cells (histology n unreported), tissue histology at 48 weeks showed no inflammation or graft-versus-host disease.
results.quote: Importantly, tissue histology at 48 weeks after IUHSCT showed no evidence of tissue inflammation or GVHD (

results.finding: Prenatally treated β-thalassemic mice had about 6% editing in total bone marrow by droplet digital PCR (n = 3).
results.quote:
Correction of
the targeted mutation was detected at a frequency of ~6% in the
total bone marrow (Table 1).

results.finding: Among 72 mice treated prenatally, zero had gross anatomical deformities, developmental abnormalities, or tumors.
results.detail: The maternal exposure experiment used fluorescent tracer particles. The reported later pregnancies were in offspring treated as fetuses.
results.quote:
No gross anatomical
deformities, developmental abnormalities, or tumors were
observed in the mice that received in utero NP treatments
(n = 72).

results.finding: Ten prenatally treated Hurler syndrome mice had approximately 22.8% liver editing at six months.
results.detail: The mouse study used the fetal vitelline vein. The proposed clinical route uses the fetal umbilical vein.

results.finding: In two dams whose fetuses received the editor, uterine editing measured 0.02% in each dam, consistent with background.
results.detail: The paper gives survival percentages for the fetal injection groups without reporting their denominators in the supplied text.
results.quote: Editing efficiencies in experimental dams (heart: 0.04%, 0.01%; liver: 0.07%, 0.21%; uteri: 0.02%, 0.02%) were comparable to uninjected control livers and hearts (0.19–0.49%) suggesting no maternal editing occurred.

results.finding: F508del CF mice (n = 9 in the ddPCR analysis) showed up to 1.5% lung CFTR editing after prenatal intravenous treatment.
results.detail: Intravenous treatment produced stronger functional correction than intra-amniotic treatment. At 8 months, nasal potential difference was assessed in 4 intravenously treated mice, 3 intra-amniotically treated mice, 12 untreated CF mice and 7 wild-type controls.
results.quote: We observed gene correction in numerous tissues relevant to CF after systemic NP treatment including the lung (up to 1.5%), pancreas (up to 8.5%), gut (up to 5.5%), skin (up to 6%), and liver (up to 0.4%).

results.finding: Prenatally treated F508del mice (n unreported for this assay) had no detectable lung mutations across 11 candidate off-target sites.
results.detail: The lung screen was restricted to candidate sites with partial sequence homology.
results.quote: The results revealed an undetectable mutation frequency at these off-target sites in both early postnatal and adult mice

results.finding: After prenatal haploidentical marrow transplantation, 4 of 4 assessable canine recipients showed stable low-level donor chimerism.
results.detail: Sensitive engraftment assays were applicable to 4 of the 10 survivors. One affected pup remained symptom-free through 18 months. The other received a postnatal transplant at 7 months because of persistent low-grade infections.
results.quote: Haploidentical IUHCT resulted in stable low level donor cell chimerism in all dogs that could be analyzed by sensitive detection methodology (4 of 10) through 18 months of follow up.

results.finding: Perinatal mortality after prenatal donor marrow transplantation was 33% among 15 treated canine fetuses.
results.detail: All perinatal deaths occurred after birth. Maternal neglect contributed to at least one death, and the exact causes of death remained unclear.
results.quote: The overall perinatal mortality of 33% (5 out of 15 injected fetuses died in the perinatal period) was related to post-natal mortality rather than in utero death.

results.finding: Five fetuses with SCID received haploidentical CD34+ cells at 21–24 weeks’ gestation.
results.detail: The reported follow-up focuses on postnatal T-cell reconstitution and clinical outcomes.
results.quote:
Between 1995 and 2001, 5 patients (IUT#1 through
IUT#5) underwent IUT with purified haploidentical
CD34+ cells at Spedali Civili Hospital, Brescia (Italy),
according to a clinical protocol approved by the Insti-
tutional Review Board.

results.finding: After prenatal hematopoietic cell transplantation for SCID, donor-derived T cells were detected in all 5 infants.
results.detail: Serial chimerism assays distinguished donor and recipient T cells. One infant had very few circulating T cells despite detectable donor-derived cells.
results.quote:
In all patients, molecular analysis at the highly poly-
morphic loci DQα and D1S80 showed the presence of
donor-derived cells among CD3+ cells that had been
positively selected using CD3-coated magnetic
microbeads.

results.finding: Four of five infants with SCID were reported in good health after prenatal hematopoietic cell transplantation.
results.detail: Postnatal transplant recipients and healthy infants served as laboratory comparators. The study did not use them to estimate a comparative effect on clinical outcomes.
results.quote:
In utero transplantation led to engraftment of donor-derived T lymphocytes
which attained normal numbers in four infants, who are in good health.

results.finding: One fetus with X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency received donor hematopoietic cells at 25 weeks’ gestation.
results.quote: Here, we report on a successful in utero transplantation (IUT) in a SCID-X1 fetus via the ultrasound-guided intravascular infusion of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) into the umbilical vein.

results.finding: In one child with X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency, circulating T cells were donor derived and subset counts normalized by 3 months.
results.detail: The 1% maternal donor-cell threshold and assessment schedule are specific to the alpha-thalassemia major trial.
results.quote: The circulating T lymphocyte count rose steadily, and the subset counts normalized between 1 and 3 months after birth.

results.finding: One child with X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency was healthy at 36 months after prenatal hematopoietic cell transplantation.
results.quote: At present, the patient is healthy; no signs of graft-versus-host-disease have been detected, and hospitalization has never been required.

results.finding: After prenatal transplantation of engineered placental mesenchymal cells, eight wild-type sheep had mean plasma FVIII activity 48.4% above controls in year 3.
results.detail: The year 3 result came from wild-type sheep. Disease-model evidence was limited to tissue findings at birth in one treated fetus with hemophilia A.
results.quote:
Evaluation
of eight animals during the 3rd year after IUTx demonstrated an overall
mean FVIII activity increase of 48.4 ± 12.3%, with two animals showing
FVIII activity between 5 and 20% (Fig.1d).

results.finding: Prenatal amniotic fluid stem cell transplantation in type III SMA mice (16 treated, 16 controls) improved performance on all three motor tests.
results.detail: The transplanted cells were unsorted and expressed mesenchymal stem cell markers. The paper reports 15 of 16 treated survivors but gives inconsistent percentages, 93.75% in the abstract and 87.5% in the Results.
results.quote: In all three behavioral tests, SMA mice with hAFSC transplantation has better performance during whole study.

results.finding: Among 13 fetal lambs given AAV9-GFP by umbilical vein injection, 84.6% survived to harvest.
results.detail: Placental pathology suggested infection in the pregnancies with fetal deaths. The open injection procedure and GFP reporter vector limit inference to a proposed human procedure and therapeutic product.
results.quote: The overall fetal survival rate to harvest was 100% for the IC-injected fetuses, 84.6% for the umbilical vein group, and 92.3% for the non-injected controls ( Figure 1 C).

results.finding: Among 46 mouse fetuses given AAV9 gene editing in utero after direct maternal sensitization, 8.7% survived to birth.
results.detail: The authors attributed the deaths to maternal immune reexposure and placental inflammation. The mouse injection route and degree of maternal sensitization differed from the proposed clinical setting.
results.quote:
with only 4 of 46 (8.7%) injected mTmG
+/–
fetuses surviving to birth following maternal direct sensitization

results.finding: In a phase 1 trial for alpha thalassemia major, all 6 fetuses received maternal hematopoietic stem cells in utero.
results.detail: The CIRM award summary describes how safety was assessed in both participants. The criterion specifically requires safety to be a primary outcome, and the summary does not identify the primary outcome.
results.quote:
In this study, six fetuses received a stem cell transplantation with donated cells from their mother during the 2
nd
trimester of pregnancy.

results.finding: BOOSTB4 (18 children overall) reported no significant short-term adverse reactions after mesenchymal stem cell–derived therapy, including 3 prenatal doses.
results.detail: Only three administrations were prenatal. The adverse-event counts were pooled across prenatal and postnatal dosing.
results.quote:
Thus, no significant short -term adverse reactions were identified 
in infants, pregnant women, or fetuses.

definition = "Treatment given to a fetus during pregnancy provides a lasting source of a function impaired by a disease that begins before birth. Gene therapy restores that function in the child\u2019s body cells. In cell therapy, donor cells engraft: they become established in the child and supply functional cells. Prenatal transplantation has restored donor-derived T cells in children with severe combined immunodeficiency. Repeated infusions of a missing enzyme supply the protein only.". Reason: The definition leaves engraftment unexplained and omits the human evidence that prenatal transplantation can restore a specific cell population.

goal.need = "Fetuses with alpha-thalassemia major usually need transfusions to survive to birth. All six children in one prenatal transplant study still needed blood every two to four weeks after birth. Sufficient donor red-cell production could free a child from those transfusions. In a retrospective cohort of 60 children with early-onset GM1 gangliosidosis, median survival was 19 months. Treatment before birth could prevent nerve damage that is already irreversible by infancy. Both uses depend on timely diagnosis and an acceptable balance of benefit and risk for mother and fetus.". Reason: The survival estimate and the frequency of transfusions after birth show the burden on children and explain what earlier treatment could change.

add statement by European Union Horizon 2020 programme, Boost Brittle Bones Before Birth, grant agreement 681045, 2015: "develop fetal MSC transplantation as a therapy for OI". Reason: The European programme names a prenatal cell-therapy goal for a skeletal disease that the existing statements do not cover.

add statement by National Institutes of Health, Office of Biotechnology Activities, notice amending the NIH Guidelines, 2001: "At the present time, there is insufficient basic and preclinical data". Reason: The dated NIH judgment records the specific objection to beginning human gene-transfer trials on the evidence available in 2001.

add case "Mesenchymal stem cell transplantation". Reason: BOOSTB4 administered mesenchymal cells prenatally to three participants with severe osteogenesis imperfecta, a distinct intervention from hematopoietic transplantation.

edit m1: criterion = "Preclinical studies demonstrate biological activity of the investigational product and the feasibility of its intended prenatal route of administration. For gene therapy, the IFeTIS consensus calls for reproducible evidence from prenatal studies in an appropriate animal model of the disease."; threshold_quote = "evaluate bioactivity, determine the feasibility of the ROA"; threshold_ref = 7; refs = [7, 5, 24]. Reason: The animal counts, survival times and donor-cell percentages are observations from individual experiments and obscure the preclinical test.

add milestone after m1: "Studies provide enough evidence to assess risk to both the pregnant patient and the fetus.". Reason: Proof of biological activity leaves a separate question before human dosing about the risks of the product and its administration to both patients.

edit m2: criterion = "At least one fetus receives the investigational gene or cell product during an ongoing pregnancy in an early-phase clinical study. Safety is a primary outcome, with monitoring of both the pregnant participant and the fetus."; set_by = "FDA early-phase cellular and gene therapy guidance, section I, and the IFeTIS consensus on maternal and fetal safety in initial trials."; set_by_kind = "regulator"; threshold_quote = "initial introduction of an investigational new drug into humans"; threshold_ref = 11; refs = [11, 21]. Reason: The criterion mixes actual administration with recruitment status and leaves the two participants in prenatal safety monitoring unnamed.

edit m3: title = "An early human study characterizes the active dose range or the safety of the feasible dose."; criterion = "An early-phase trial characterizes the range of biologically active or optimal effective doses against its prespecified activity and toxicity measures. When production or delivery limits the doses that can be given, the trial establishes the specified target exposure or characterizes safety at the feasible dose or doses."; set_by = "FDA guidance on early-phase cellular and gene therapy trials, section IV.A.1, Dose Exploration."; set_by_kind = "regulator"; threshold_quote = "characterizing the safety profile of the feasible dose or doses"; threshold_ref = 11; refs = [11]. Reason: The 1% donor-cell endpoint measures engraftment, while FDA describes a separate dose-exploration objective and allows for a single feasible dose.

add milestone after m3: "The prenatal product meets its prespecified measure of biological activity in a human recipient.". Reason: A separate human activity milestone gives protocol-defined engraftment and gene-function measurements an appropriate test before definitive evidence of benefit.

edit m4: criterion = "Two adequate and well-controlled clinical investigations, or one such investigation plus confirmatory evidence when FDA accepts that combination, establish effectiveness for the proposed prenatal indication. The endpoint measures how the patient feels, functions or survives, or is a validated surrogate for that benefit. The effect size, analysis and follow-up are specific to the disease and product."; threshold_quote = "one adequate and well-controlled clinical study plus confirmatory evidence is sufficient to establish effectiveness."; threshold_ref = 7; refs = [7]. Reason: The final evidence milestone should specify what demonstrates benefit without including verdicts on an early transplant study or a registered trial.
remove not found 3. Reason: The full alpha-thalassemia trial report is available as PMC13382725 and gives the prespecified engraftment endpoint, stopping decision and postnatal transfusion frequency.
